summary:
Aruba is a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It has its own criminal code and parliament; defence and foreign affairs sit with the Kingdom, and the Supreme Court of the Netherlands is the final appellate instance.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

The Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including "heterosexual or homosexual orientation". Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed.

Marriages registered in the Netherlands have had to be recognised in Aruba since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007. On 8 September 2016 the Aruban Parliament voted 11-5, with four abstentions, to create registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples, carrying spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024. Same-sex marriage has been legal since the 12 July 2024 ruling of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands, which upheld an Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's representation acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth in Aruba, who were stigmatised as disordered.

Harassment has been documented. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge between 2004 and 2007, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognise same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights.

The Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba is quoted: "Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official." Specific gay bars and clubs operate in Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly.
tangentialFactors:
The Aruba Tourism Authority markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling safe, secure and welcome as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketing rather than independent evidence.

Aruba was the first island in the Caribbean to grant civil partnerships to same-sex couples; at the time, neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions. It is described as having a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao.
localsOnly:
Same-sex adoption is legal.

The civil-partnership campaign ran for two and a half years and was sponsored by openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes, who introduced the bill in August 2016; an Igualdad Aruba petition gathered nearly 20,000 signatures.

Local advocacy organisations include Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and the Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Criminal Code's enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only. No source in the inventory records enforcement data, prosecutions or case law under Articles 2:61 and 2:62, and none addresses whether gender identity or expression is read into Article 1:221 by interpretation.

The 12 July 2024 ruling is framed around discrimination based on sexual orientation; how it applies to transgender people's marriages, and the procedures for changing gender markers, are not sourced.

The inventory contains no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation, and no entry, visa or airport screening provisions specific to transgender travellers. Facilities law, including bathroom and changing-room access, is not addressed.
